s: 14.0 million people (21% of population) were in relative poverty in 2022/23
d: JRF UK Poverty 2024: 14.4 million people lived in poverty, including 4.2 million children (29%) and 2.0 million pensioners. Poverty concentrated in households with children, disabled people (31%) and lone parents (44%).

s: 7.6 million NHS waiting list (June 2024), 6.4 million patients
d: NHS England RTT: ~7.6 million incomplete referral-to-treatment pathways, the longest backlog on record with millions waiting over 18 weeks for treatment.

s: Over 109,000 households in temporary accommodation (2024)
d: Statutory homelessness in England April-June 2024: tens of thousands of households owed a main homelessness duty; temporary accommodation at record levels. Rough sleeping snapshot autumn 2023 counted thousands sleeping rough, heavily concentrated in London.
src: gov.uk MHCLG Statutory Homelessness / Rough Sleeping 2023-24

s: Around 3.8 million people feel lonely often or always
d: ONS Measuring Loneliness: a substantial minority of adults report chronic loneliness, with younger adults and those on low incomes disproportionately affected.

s: 1 in 5 people (20%) in relative poverty after housing costs
d: Scottish Government poverty stats: around 1 million people, including 240,000 children, live in relative poverty; child poverty persistent in Glasgow and Dundee.

s: 122,000 emergency food parcels (Trussell, Apr-Sep 2024)
d: Trussell Trust: food banks in its Scottish network distributed 122,000 emergency food parcels in the first half of 2024; Scotland has among the highest per-capita food bank use in the UK.

s: 29% of children in Wales in relative poverty (after housing costs)
d: Bevan Foundation / Welsh Govt: roughly 190,000 children in Wales live in relative poverty, with the highest rates in the South Wales valleys and post-industrial communities.

s: 83,000 emergency food parcels (Trussell, Apr-Sep 2024)
d: Trussell Trust: Welsh food banks distributed close to 83,000 emergency food parcels in the first half of 2024, with particular pressure in Swansea, Newport and the valleys.

p: Food bank use in Northern Ireland
s: 35,000 emergency food parcels (Trussell, Apr-Sep 2024)
d: Trussell Trust: food banks in Northern Ireland distributed almost 35,000 emergency food parcels in the first half of 2024; demand rising fastest here of any UK nation.

s: 2.6 million emergency food parcels distributed in Trussell network (year to Mar 2024)
d: Trussell Trust end-of-year stats: 2.6 million emergency food parcels handed out across the UK, a near-tripling since 2019, with 63% going to households with children.

s: Male life expectancy 73.1 years (2022-24), lowest in England
d: ONS: Blackpool has the lowest male life expectancy in England (73.1 years) and high rates of mortality from alcohol, drugs and suicide — markers of deep social isolation and deprivation on the Lancashire coast.

s: Around 47% of children in Middlesbrough live in poverty
d: End Child Poverty / Loughborough: Middlesbrough and surrounding Teesside local authorities have among the highest child poverty rates in England, exceeding 45%, driven by low wages and benefit cuts.

s: Around 39% of children in Hull in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Hull has one of the highest child poverty rates in Yorkshire, with deprivation concentrated in the north and east of the city and strong dependence on food banks.

p: Lowest female life expectancy in UK
s: Female life expectancy 78.0 years (2022-24), lowest in UK
d: ONS: Glasgow City continues to have the lowest female life expectancy in the UK (78.0 years); the city also has the highest drug-death rate in Europe, signalling acute social fragmentation.

s: Around 38% of children in Nottingham in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Nottingham has one of the highest child poverty rates in the East Midlands, alongside Stoke-on-Trent and Leicester in the regional cluster of need.

s: Around 35% of children in Stoke live in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty / IMD: Stoke-on-Trent is among the most deprived local authorities in England, with high child poverty and reliance on food banks across the six towns.
src: End Child Poverty Coalition / ONS IMD

s: London accounts for ~40% of England's rough sleepers
d: gov.uk rough sleeping snapshot: London contains a disproportionate share of England's rough-sleeping population; inner-London boroughs such as Newham have the highest per-capita counts.

s: Life expectancy gap of ~10 years vs poorest boroughs
d: ONS: the Royal Borough has among the highest life expectancy in England while neighbouring deprived boroughs are ~10 years lower — the starkest inequality gradient in the country.

s: Around 40% of children in Birmingham in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Birmingham, Europe's largest local authority by population, has child poverty above 40% in many wards, with concentrated deprivation in the east and north.

s: Around 44% of children in Manchester in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Manchester has one of the highest child poverty rates among core cities, with inner-city wards exceeding 45% and widening inequality against its affluent suburbs.

s: Around 33% of children in Leeds in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Leeds shows a sharp geographic divide — child poverty above 40% in inner-south and east wards, far lower in the north and west.

s: Around 38% of children in Liverpool in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Liverpool retains some of the highest deprivation scores in the North West, with child poverty clustered in the north and central wards.

s: Around 27% of children in Bristol in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Bristol has a lower city-wide rate but extreme localised deprivation in Lawrence Weston and Filwood contrasted with affluent Clifton.

s: Around 38% of children in Bradford in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Bradford, a young and fast-growing city, has high child poverty concentrated in the Bradford Moor and Bowling wards.

s: Around 30% of children in Sheffield in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Sheffield shows deprivation concentrated in the north-east (Firvale, Burngreave) against more affluent west wards.

s: Around 34% of children in Newcastle in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Newcastle has significant child poverty in the west and east central wards, part of the wider North East deprivation pattern.

s: Around 28% of children in Cardiff in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty / Welsh Govt: Cardiff has rising child poverty concentrated in the south and east of the city (Butetown, Splott, Ely).

s: Around 25% of children in NI in relative poverty
d: Northern Ireland poverty stats: Belfast has the highest deprivation concentrations in NI, with child poverty clustered in west and north Belfast.

s: Around 18% of children in Bath in relative poverty
d: End Child Poverty: Bath's city-wide rate is low but there are pockets of deprivation in Twerton and Radstock, with isolation among an ageing population a local concern.
